Processing and analysis of MALDI-imaging data

John Abbey1,2*

1Department for Quantitative Biomedicine, University of Zurich
2Institute for Molecular Health Sciences, ETH Zurich

*john.abbey@uzh.ch

6 September 2023

Abstract

This R package supports the processing and analysis of highly multiplexed MALDI-imaging data. The data handling capabilities (import, pre-processing, export) build heavily on the R package Cardinal, designed for general Mass Spectrometry Imaging data. The main functionality of this package includes reliable data processing, extensive quality control and data analysis. First, data is processing using a novel approach involving the construction of metapeaks to account for mass shift and the presence of isotopic peaks. Then image-level and spatial quality control statistics, such as computing Geary’s C scores can be computed for every marker. Furthermore, spatial analysis can be performed on the high-dimensional images, including constructing variograms and a variety of clustering algorithms. The package also supports dimensionality reduction methods, including PCA, NMF and UMAP. Additionally, the package supports image visualisation from cytomapper (and cytoviewer) through the construction of a CytoImageList object. As such, once the data is coerced to this format, many of the analysis techniques that are applicable to CytoImageList can be applied.

Package

maldipackage 0.1.0

1 Introduction

Cardinal

1.1 Overview

The maldipackage package exports functions and example data to perform the following analyses:

  1. Read in raw datadata
  2. Perform data pre-processing
  3. Data processing
  4. Visualisation of processed targeted images
  5. Dimensionality reduction of processed targeted images
  6. Community detection

To highlight the usability of these function, the maldipackage package also exports a number of test data files.

1.1.1 MALDI-imaging

2 Read in raw data and panel

The raw imaging data can be read into R using the readMSIData function from Cardinal.

imzML_path <- system.file("extdata/Example_data.imzML", package = "maldipackage")
rawFile <- Cardinal::readMSIData(imzML_path)

The readPanel function can be used to read a .csv file into R. containing the information for the mass of the peptide tag and the molecular target into R.

panel_path <- system.file("extdata/ref_list.csv", package = "maldipackage")
panel <- maldipackage::readPanel(panel_path)

3 Example data

If you want to see how the package functions on test data, or do not have access to the required data yet, a good place to start is by loading in the example data from the github repository. The maldipackage package contains example data generated by the RapiFlex imaging system. The following section gives an overview of these files.

These files are accessible via:

path <- system.file("extdata", package = "maldipackage")
list.files(path, recursive = TRUE)
## [1] "Example_data.ibd"   "Example_data.imzML" "ref_list.csv"

By default, the imaging data is read into a MSImagingExperiment object. Here, the extracted channel-specific intensities are stored in the ??? slot.

4 Data pre-processing

When acquiring the raw data, the resulting spectra can often be noisy and messy. To correct for this, some pre-processing steps are required. This can be done simply using the preProcess function from this package, which can be implemented as follows.

pre <- preProcess(rawFile, cores = 2)

This function is a wrapper for the Cardinal functions normalize, smoothSignal and reduceBaseline, using common parameters and methods for each function. For more flexibility in your pre-processing, it is recommended to directly use the Cardinal functions. Here, we use total ion current (TIC) as the normalisation method of choice, Gaussian smoothing for spectral smoothing and local minimum baseline reduction.

pre <- rawFile %>%
    Cardinal::normalize(method = "tic") %>%
    smoothSignal(method = "gaussian", plot = FALSE) %>%
    reduceBaseline(method = "locmin") %>%
    process(BPPARAM = MulticoreParam(workers = 2))

5 Data processing

Full processing of the pre-processed MALDI-imaging data can be performed using the peakDetection, metapeakGeneration and assignMetapeaks functions in series.

5.1 Peak Detection

The first step of processing is to identify peaks in the pre-processed spectra. This function is essentially a wrapper for Cardinal::peakPick, and uses the median adaptive deviation (MAD) peak detection algorithm for robust noise evaluation.

detected <- maldipackage::peakDetection(pre, snr = 3, cores = 2)

5.2 Metapeak generation

Once peakDetection has been performed, the detected peaks per pixel can be used to generate metapeaks. Here, metapeaks are defined as single peaks that correspond to clusters of peaks that contain information on the same molecular species. The function used to generate these metapeaks is metapeakGeneration. This step is implemented to account for loss of signal through technical shift and isotopic peaks in the spectra. Inside this function, metapeaks are constructed by

  1. Obtaining the number of pixels in which each detected peak is present.
  2. Gaussian smoothing over the spectrum
  3. Watershed algorithm to cluster detected peaks
  4. Filter peaks present in less than a given threshold of pixels, which can be controlled using the threshold parameter.

It is important to note that metapeaks are not restricted to targeted peaks. Many of the metapeaks generated will be formed by signal that is from untargeted peaks.

metapeaks <- maldipackage::metapeakGeneration(detected)

5.3 Assigning metapeaks

The final step of processing is to assign metapeaks to the reference list of masses that was loaded in using the readPanel function. This is performed using the assignMetapeaks function. The output of this function is a list of lists, containing primarily IntensityDF, the channel-specific intensities, SpatialCoords, the spatial coordinates and CorrespondenceMatrix, a data frame describing the assignment of metapeaks to reference peaks. This assignment can be controlled via the mz_threshold parameter, which has a default of 1m/z.

You may notice that some of the expected peaks in the reference list will not appear in the output. This is likely due to either a lack of signal, resulting in the metapeak not passing the filter threshold during metapeakGeneration, or the metapeak center being out of range for assignment to a reference peak during assignMetapeaks. These parameters can be adjusted to improve results.

processed <- maldipackage::assignMetapeaks(metapeaks, refList = panel, pre = pre)

6 Visualisation of processed data

6.1 Cytomapper

This package supports visualisation of MALDI images through the cytomapper framework developed by Eling et al (reference). In order to use the plotPixels function, the data must first be coerced to a CytoImageList object using the asCytoImageList function from this package.

library(cytomapper)
cil <- asCytoImageList(processed)

Now the channels can be visualised using the plotPixels function. Single channel and multichannel imaging is supported using this format.

cytomapper::plotPixels(image = cil, colour_by = "HLA.ABC")

plotPixels(cil, colour_by = c("HLA.ABC", "CD98", "beta.actin"), 
           legend = list(colour_by.title.cex = 0.7), 
           scale_bar = list(length = 4, lwidth = 0.5, margin = c(1,1)),
           image_title = list(margin = c(1, 1)))

6.2 Cytoviewer

Additionally, the images can be visualised using the cytoviewer R Shiny app developed by Meyer et al 2023 (ref). cytoviewer allows interactive visualistion of multi-channel images, supporting visualisation of up to 6 channels. It should be noted that the cell-level functionality of cytomapper and cytoviewer are not applicable for our data, since single-cell resolution is not yet possible.

library(cytoviewer)
cytoviewer(cil)
Shiny applications not supported in static R Markdown documents

7 Dimensionality Reduction

7.1 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Dimensionality reduction techniques can be helpful in revealing the overall structure of the data, especially during the exploratory phase of data analysis. This package explicitly supports PCA, NMF and UMAP.

PCA is a very commonly used techniques which linearly separates the data according to the orthogonal dimensions with greatest variance. This can be performed using the pca function. This function wraps the irlba implementation of PCA, requiring a set seed. This takes the targeted intensity dataframe as the main argument. The number of components, aswell as some plotting functions can also be chosen as arguments.

Once this is performed, the loadings for each component can be accessed under my_pca$rotation.

my_pca <- maldipackage::pca(processed$IntensityDF, comp = 5, scree = TRUE)

for (i in 1:ncol(my_pca$x)){
  maldipackage::imageChannel(my_pca$x, coords = processed$SpatialCoords, channel_number = i)
}

7.2 Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF)

In practice, NMF often performs better than PCA in terms of decomposing the major dimensions of the data. NMF gives parts-based representation of the data, w. NMF can be performed using the nmf function provided by this package.

my_nmf <- maldipackage::nmf(processed$IntensityDF, comp = 5)
## 
## iter |      tol 
## ---------------
##    1 | 8.98e-01
##    2 | 7.60e-02
##    3 | 1.29e-02
##    4 | 4.05e-03
##    5 | 2.61e-03
##    6 | 2.65e-03
##    7 | 2.43e-03
##    8 | 1.67e-03
##    9 | 9.81e-04
##   10 | 4.19e-04
##   11 | 2.23e-04
##   12 | 1.71e-04
##   13 | 1.38e-04
##   14 | 1.16e-04
##   15 | 1.01e-04
##   16 | 8.92e-05
# visualise the factored dimensions
for (i in 1:ncol(my_pca$x)){
  maldipackage::imageChannel(my_nmf$w, coords = processed$SpatialCoords, channel_number = i)
}

7.3 Uniform Manifold Approximate Projection (UMAP)

UMAP is a non-linear dimensionality technique that embeds high dimensional data into two dimensions, providing an overview of the global structure of the data.

This package includes the computeUMAP function, which computes the UMAP using the uwot package implementation.

my_umap <-computeUMAP(processed$IntensityDF)

One of the ways in which UMAP can be used is to display single-channel intensity information on top of the UMAP.

# create data frame
umap_df <- cbind(my_umap, processed$IntensityDF)

# plot UMAP with channel intensity
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(umap_df) +
  geom_point(aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = HLA.ABC), alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +
  labs(title = "HLA.DR",
       x = "UMAP 1",
       y = "UMAP 2",
       color = "Intensity")

8 Community detection

The maldipackage exports the louvain_cluster function to detect the spatial community of each pixel. Here, each pixe is clustered based on its interactions as defined by a spatial object graph.

In more detail, the spatial community detection procedure is as follows:

  1. Create an igraph object.

  2. Perform community detection using the louvain algorithm.

  3. Store the community IDs in a vector.

clusters <- louvain_cluster(processed$IntensityDF)

One of the ways in which these clusters can be visualised is to display the cluster memberships over the UMAP. This shows us how cluster formation corresponds to the global structure of the data.

# create data frame
cluster_df <- cbind(my_umap, clusters)

# plot UMAP with channel intensity
ggplot(cluster_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = clusters)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = "Cluster Membership") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Cluster Memberships on Spatial Coordinates",
       x = "x",
       y = "y")

Perhaps more informatively, the cluster memberships can be plotted onto the spatial coordinates, revealing how the spatial context of the tissue informs the cluster membership.

# create data frame
cluster_coords <- cbind(processed$SpatialCoords, clusters)

# ggplot spatial distribution of clusters
ggplot(cluster_coords, aes(x = x, y = y, color = clusters)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_color_discrete(name="Cluster Membership") +
  #scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "Cluster Membership") + # alternative colour set for clustering
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Cluster Memberships on Spatial Coordinates",
       x = "X Coordinate",
       y = "Y Coordinate")

9 Contributions

Pierre Bost conceptualised the metapeak generation step for data processing, as well as being instrumental in developing the architecture of the pipeline.
Nils Eling assisted in designing and developing the structure of the package, as well as assisting in integrating the package with cytomapper, while Lasse Meyer has contributed to integrating the package with cytoviewer.
